meta.research_area: 3 of 5: identity/permission handling in multi-agent AI frameworks
meta.consuming_project: meept (pure-Go, single-daemon self-hosted agent platform; needs grouped-agent, per-group access to tools/memory/filesystem/cluster resources; constraint: no heavyweight external services)
meta.method: 4 parallel research leaves (web_search + web_extract); every claim carries a URL actually fetched or surfaced by search

mcp.authorization_model: MCP authorization is transport-level OAuth 2.1 for HTTP-based transports, OPTIONAL overall (stdio transports SHOULD NOT use it and pull credentials from the environment). Introduced in the 2025-03-26 spec, which made MCP servers OAuth participants (implicitly treating server+AS as one) with OAuth 2.1, RFC 8414 auth-server metadata, and RFC 7591 dynamic client registration (SHOULD). The 2025-06-18 revision recast MCP servers strictly as OAuth 2.1 RESOURCE SERVERS (PR #338), not authorization servers: servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) to advertise authorization_servers, MUST serve/clients MUST use RFC 8414 AS metadata, servers MUST set WWW-Authenticate on 401 pointing at the resource-metadata URL, and clients MUST implement RFC 8707 resource indicators (the 'resource' parameter in authorization AND token requests, set to the MCP server's canonical URI) to prevent confused-deputy/token theft across servers. The 2025-11-25 revision added a Scope Selection Strategy (prefer the WWW-Authenticate 'scope' param, fall back to PRM scopes_supported), a Scope Challenge Handling / step-up flow (403 + WWW-Authenticate error=insufficient_scope with resource_metadata), and replaced DCR as the default with OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents (SEP-991; CIMD SHOULD, DCR demoted to MAY and marked deprecated for backwards compatibility). SEP-985 later relaxed WWW-Authenticate from MUST to SHOULD for servers (clients still MUST parse it and fall back to probing well-known URIs).

per_tool_authorization.summary: The MCP spec defines ONLY server-level (resource-server) authorization. It does NOT define any per-tool permission model, does not add scopes to the Tool schema, and defines no standard scope vocabulary at all — scopes_supported is server-defined free text. All tool-level machinery exists only as proposals and working-group discussions, none adopted: SEP-1880 (Tool.authorization.scopes field, closed, never merged), SEP-1881 (Scope-Filtered Tool Discovery, proposal), SEP-1385 (Tool 'requires' field incl. permission/scope requirement types, proposal), SEP-835 (default scopes / scope selection strategy — largely landed in 2025-11-25 as Scope Selection Strategy, but without a scope vocabulary), Discussion #810 (MCP permission system via scopes, 2025). The Feb 17 2026 Auth WG Tool Scopes meeting (Discussion #2266) explicitly concluded that static per-tool scope lists have repeatedly failed to reach the spec because of scope-hierarchy complexity ('the client must remain dumb'; all scope resolution belongs server-side), and deferred pre-flight/protocol work to the Fine-Grained Authorization (FGA) working group while SDK scope-challenge support proceeds first (started in TypeScript SDK, issue typescript-sdk#1151). Enforcement of per-tool permissions is therefore entirely application/vendor-specific.

scope_debate.summary: The spec deliberately stays at server-level scope granularity: it defines NO scope vocabulary (no standard scope names or profile), letting each server define its own scopes_supported, and relies on WWW-Authenticate challenges + step-up for incremental authorization. SEP-835 ('default scopes', scopes_supported as the minimal bootstrap set, incremental elevation via challenges) was the main spec-level scope work and was refined in the Auth WG (Sept 2025 meeting notes, Discussion #1743). The community clearly wants finer granularity: vendor posts (WorkOS: 'scopes have to be per tool, not per server'; Scalekit: per-tool scope validation and scope-action maps; Auth0: per-tool authorization policies with tool:* permissions) all implement per-tool gating as an application-layer pattern. Spec-side attempts (SEP-1880 tool-level scopes, SEP-1881 scope-filtered discovery) remain unmerged; the Feb 2026 Tool Scopes WG concluded tool scope lists don't work statically (GitHub-style scope hierarchies differ per AS) and split the problem: SDK scope-challenge ergonomics first, protocol pre-flight hints later under the FGA working group. Net: per-tool authorization is a de-facto best practice implemented ad hoc, not a protocol guarantee.

go_sdk.status: Official, actively maintained Go SDK, maintained in collaboration with Google. Latest stable v1.8.0 (released ~Sep 14, 2026, per releases page); v1.7.0 (Jul 28) added full support for the 2026-07-28 protocol revision (stateless _meta model, server/discover, MRTR) and negotiates down to 2025-11-25 / 2025-06-18 / 2025-03-26 / 2024-11-05. pkg.go.dev shows v1.8.0, Go >= 1.25, Apache-2.0/MIT/CC-BY-4.0.
go_sdk.auth: Implements auth in three packages: mcp (server-side RequireBearerToken middleware checking expiration + scopes against RequireBearerTokenOptions.Scopes, sets WWW-Authenticate per RFC 9728, exposes TokenInfo via req.Extra.TokenInfo / auth.TokenInfoFromContext), auth (OAuth primitives, AuthorizationCodeHandler with client-id-metadata-documents, pre-registered clients, DCR, RFC 9207, refresh + insufficient_scope step-up, ClockSkew/AllowMissingExpiration options), and oauthex (ProtectedResourceMetadata types, RFC 9728/8707 audience comparison helper MatchesResource). Client side OAuth is flagged experimental (per version-compat table footnote for v1.4.0+). NO per-tool authorization API — tools declare no scopes; enforcement is whatever the TokenVerifier/handler does.
go_sdk.api_shape: mcp.NewClient/mcp.NewServer(&mcp.Implementation{Name,Version}, options) -> Client.Connect(ctx, transport, opts) -> *ClientSession / Server.Connect -> *ServerSession; typed request/response via generics: mcp.AddTool(server, &mcp.Tool{...}, handlerFn(ctx, req *mcp.CallToolRequest, input Input) (*mcp.CallToolResult, Output, error)); transports: StdioTransport, CommandTransport, StreamableHTTPTransport (+ StreamableHTTPHandler, StreamableHTTPOptions.Stateless for 2026-07-28), InMemoryTransports, jsonrpc2 for custom transports; sessions expose CallTool, Close, Wait. Both legacy initialize handshake and the 2026-07-28 stateless model supported transparently.
go_sdk.maintenance: Active: 164 commits to main since v1.7.0; regular releases; SEP-driven feature flow (SEP-2350 scope accumulation, SEP-2207 refresh guidance, SEP-2468 issuer mix-up mitigation, SEP-2575/2577).

mcp.maturity: Spec: stable and actively revised (four dated revisions through 2026-07-28, SEP governance process, dedicated Auth WG + FGA WG). Authorization at server level is settled; per-tool authorization is NOT settled and was explicitly deferred. Go SDK: production-grade (v1.8.0, v1 line, Google co-maintained, full spec coverage incl. 2026-07-28 stateless), with mature server-side token-verification middleware and recently stabilized but still-flagged-experimental client-side OAuth. The per-tool/per-scope ecosystem (SEP-1880/1881, SDK scope-challenge ergonomics) is early: TS SDK issue-level feature requests, closed unmerged SEPs.
mcp.fit_assessment: Good fit with one caveat. For a single-daemon Go platform like meept (no external auth services): (a) as an MCP CLIENT connecting to user-configured servers, the go-sdk gives stdio + streamable HTTP transports and sessions out of the box — stdio needs no OAuth at all (spec says use env credentials), matching meept's existing mcp_servers.json5 pattern; client-side OAuth for remote servers is functional but experimental, so treat remote-OAuth servers as best-effort. (b) as an MCP SERVER (exposing meept tools to external agents), RequireBearerToken middleware + PRM handler make RFC-compliant resource-server auth a thin layer over meept's existing internal/auth key store — but the spec only gives you server-level gating; per-tool permissions must be built in-application (a simple per-tool required-scope/permission check in the tool handler, the same pattern every vendor uses), and no standard scope vocabulary exists so scope names are yours to define. Avoid adopting the 2026-07-28 stateless protocol initially — negotiate down (SDK default) since it deprecates roots/sampling/logging that some clients still use. Overall: adopt the SDK for transport/session plumbing; implement authorization as thin server-level token checking plus in-process per-tool permission checks rather than standing up an external OAuth AS.

openai_agents_sdk.identity_model: No built-in multi-tenant or per-user identity/auth model. Tools execute with the host process's privileges; per-run application state (including anything identity-like) is carried in the caller-supplied RunContextWrapper.context, which the SDK explicitly says is for 'application state and dependencies you already have locally', not security enforcement. Model/auth credentials are supplied by the developer (OPENAI_API_KEY / CODEX_API_KEY), and hosted tools (web search, file search, code interpreter, hosted MCP) execute on OpenAI servers under the developer's OpenAI account. Authentication is effectively delegated to the underlying Responses API / model provider; the SDK has no identity layer of its own.
openai_agents_sdk.tool_scoping_mechanism: Tool scoping is a static, per-agent constructor parameter: each Agent is configured with a tools list (function tools, hosted tools like WebSearchTool/FileSearchTool/HostedMCPTool, agents-as-tools) plus optional mcp_servers/mcp_config. There is no central registry with per-user ACLs — whatever list you pass to the Agent constructor is exactly what that agent can call. Handoffs are themselves represented as tools (transfer_to_<agent_name>) and can be dynamically enabled/disabled via the handoff() is_enabled flag; ToolSearchTool (hosted) can defer loading large tool surfaces until runtime, but that is token optimization, not authorization.
openai_agents_sdk.permission_gating: What exists today is guardrails + human-in-the-loop pauses, not permissions: (1) Input guardrails run only on the first agent's initial user input (parallel by default, or blocking run_in_parallel=False so the agent never executes on tripwire); (2) Output guardrails run only on the agent producing the final output; (3) Tool guardrails (tool_input_guardrail / tool_output_guardrail decorators) run on every guarded function-tool invocation, e.g. blocking args containing secrets; (4) Human approval is modeled as a paused/resumed run ('treat approvals as paused runs, not as new turns'). Critically, a handoff transfers full conversation control (and the recipient sees the history unless an input_filter removes items) — no credentials, scopes, or permission sets transfer because none exist at the SDK level; the docs even note is_enabled is evaluated before arguments and 'cannot authorize values inside an argument-bearing handoff', pushing authorization into developer on_handoff callbacks.
openai_agents_sdk.maturity: Production-ready and actively developed (successor to Swarm), with a deliberately small primitive set (agents, handoffs, guardrails) plus built-in tracing. Guardrails including the newer tool guardrails are documented as first-class, but the permission/identity dimension is explicitly left to the developer.
openai_agents_sdk.fit_assessment: Good conceptual fit for a single-daemon Go platform with no heavyweight external services: the architecture confirms that per-user authorization is the host application's job, which matches meept's internal/auth + internal/security layers — the SDK adds no dependency and offers no conflicting identity service to adopt. Its useful patterns to port: static per-agent tool lists (map directly to meept's per-employee tool exposure), tripwire-style input/output/tool guardrails as pre/post hooks in the agent loop, and approvals-as-paused-runs (maps to meept's plans approve/reject + ACP human-permission relay). Its handoff model (full conversation + history transfer, no scoped credentials) is a model of what NOT to do if cross-agent privilege transfer is ever needed.

semantic_kernel.identity_model: No built-in identity, tenant, or per-user auth model. Identity is delegated entirely to the host application: Semantic Kernel is constructed via dependency injection, and the docs' own permission example shows the app checking 'the permissions of the person' inside a filter. There is no SK-managed principal, token, or multi-tenant construct; whatever user context exists must be threaded through the app's own DI services or filter contexts.
semantic_kernel.tool_scoping_mechanism: Scoping is plugin/function registration per Kernel instance: plugins (groups of functions, importable from native code, OpenAPI specs, or MCP servers) are added to a Kernel, and every function in that kernel is exposed to function calling. There is no per-agent built-in ACL — the granularity is which plugins you import into which kernel (e.g., building a separate kernel per agent or per user is a host-app pattern, not an SK feature). Plugins play well with DI, so constructor-injected services (db connections, http clients) are the intended place to carry scoped credentials.
semantic_kernel.permission_gating: The permission/approval story is the filter pipeline: three filter types — Function Invocation Filter (runs on every KernelFunction invocation; can inspect function + arguments, override the result before/after, block by not calling next), Prompt Render Filter, and Auto Function Invocation Filter (scoped to automatic function calling, sees chat history + all functions + iteration counters, can set context.Terminate). Microsoft's documented human-in-the-loop pattern is a function invocation filter that prompts for consent before sensitive calls (e.g., DynamicsPlugin.create_order) and, on refusal, sets the FunctionResult to 'The order creation was not approved by the user' so the model gets a meaningful message instead of retrying. The filters doc explicitly frames this as enterprise security: 'filters are leveraged to validate permissions before an approval flow begins... only a select group of people will be able to kick off the process.' This is all DIY middleware, not a declarative permission system: filters are stable (graduated from experimental; IFunctionFilter -> IFunctionInvocationFilter in v1.10.0), but approval flows, consent prompts, and permission checks are developer-written code.
semantic_kernel.maturity: Mature and enterprise-oriented: filters are GA (the migration doc states the latest filter version 'has graduated from experimental status and is now officially released as a stable feature'), available across .NET/Python/Java with per-language pivots. However, the human-in-the-loop and permission material is presented as example patterns rather than built-in product features — no declarative policy engine, no per-user grant model.
semantic_kernel.fit_assessment: Moderate fit for a single-daemon Go platform: SK itself is .NET/Python/Java, so nothing is directly adoptable — but its architecture validates meept's existing shape. The function-invocation-filter pipeline is essentially Go middleware around tool dispatch (maps cleanly onto internal/tools registry wrapping + internal/acp human-permission relay), the per-kernel plugin scoping maps to per-employee tool registries, and 'identity lives in the host app' confirms building multi-user gating on internal/auth rather than expecting the framework to supply it. The documented consent-filter pattern (meaningful refusal message back to the model so it doesn't blind-retry) is a directly portable detail. No heavyweight external services are implied by the pattern; risk is only reimplementing order-dependence semantics (SK warns DI-registered filter order is unpredictable; direct Kernel properties give deterministic order — the Go equivalent should use an explicit ordered slice).

langgraph.identity_model: End-user identity is established at the platform layer, not in graph code: an @auth.authenticate handler runs as middleware on every request, validates credentials, and returns a MinimalUserDict with an 'identity' field plus arbitrary custom fields (roles, org IDs, OAuth tokens). The resolved user is injected into graph execution as config['configurable']['langgraph_auth_user'] so nodes can act on behalf of the user. Without a custom handler, LangGraph sees only the API-key owner and requests are not scoped to end-users. Conversation state is scoped per thread via configurable.thread_id, and per-user long-term data is namespaced in stores.
langgraph.tool_scoping_mechanism: Per-agent/per-model tool scoping is done by binding tools to the model: ChatModel.bind_tools(tools) restricts which tools a given model instance can call, and create_agent(model, tools=[...]) scopes the agent's toolset at construction. The Tools guide explicitly documents dynamic tool selection/filtering as the way to adapt the toolset to 'authentication state, user permissions, feature flags, or conversation stage' (filtering pre-registered tools or runtime tool registration). For LangGraph graphs, tool execution is handled by ToolNode. There is no declarative permission object on tools themselves; scoping is by which tools you bind plus application logic.
langgraph.permission_gating: Human-in-the-loop approval is first-class. (1) Dynamic interrupts: interrupt() can be placed anywhere, including inside a @tool function, pausing execution whenever the tool is invoked; the caller resumes with Command(resume=...) and can approve, edit arguments, or cancel; requires a checkpointer. (2) HITL middleware: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={...}) defines a per-tool policy (e.g. 'write_file': True, 'execute_sql': {'allowed_decisions': ['approve','reject']}, 'read_data': False) with four decision types: approve, edit, reject, respond; state persists via LangGraph persistence so runs pause and resume later. (3) Static breakpoints (interrupt_before/interrupt_after at compile or run time) exist but docs say they are not recommended for HITL — debugging-oriented.
langgraph.memory_isolation: Long-term memory uses BaseStore implementations (InMemoryStore, PostgresStore, MongoDBStore, RedisStore, UpstashStore) where memories are namespaced by arbitrary tuples, conventionally (user_id, 'memories'); thread-scoped state lives in the checkpointer keyed by thread_id. Isolation is by convention, not enforcement — but the platform auth layer can enforce it: an @auth.on.store handler can force the namespace prefix to the authenticated user's identity (reference.langchain.com Auth example scopes all store operations to namespace[0] == ctx.user.identity), and @auth.on.threads.* filters make threads private to their owner. Cross-thread/cross-user visibility depends on the app setting namespaces and filters correctly.
langgraph.platform_auth: LangGraph Platform (Agent Server / LangSmith deployments) provides custom authentication and resource-level access control: a python auth file declared in langgraph.json ('auth': {'path': 'src/security/auth.py:auth'}) is loaded server-side. @auth.authenticate validates every request; @auth.on authorization handlers receive an AuthContext (user, permissions, resource, action) and value, and can (a) stamp metadata on created resources (e.g. owner = user identity), (b) return filters limiting reads/searches to matching resources, or (c) reject with HTTP 403. Handlers resolve most-specific-first (@auth.on.threads.create > @auth.on.threads > @auth.on); supported resources include threads, assistants, crons, and store. Caveats: custom auth is available only on LangSmith SaaS or Enterprise self-hosted deployments and was Python-only at introduction; if no global handler is set, unmatched requests are accepted (default-allow unless a default-deny handler is registered).
langgraph.maturity: Core HITL/persistence/interrupt machinery is mature and production-oriented (resumable months later, cross-machine). Platform-level custom auth is newer and narrower: Python-first, gated to LangSmith SaaS/Enterprise self-hosted tiers, with store-action authorization added after the initial threads/assistants/crons support.
langgraph.fit_assessment: Strong source of design patterns, weak as a dependency: the portable ideas are (1) request-level authn middleware returning an identity dict injected into every turn, (2) resource-level authorization handlers that stamp ownership metadata and return read filters (owner-scoped threads), (3) namespace-prefix forcing on stores, (4) per-agent tool binding as the scoping primitive, and (5) interrupt/resume approval with approve/edit/reject decisions backed by persisted state. None of this is reusable from Go directly (LangGraph Platform is a Python deployment runtime); a single-daemon Go platform would re-implement the middleware + owner-filter + interrupt-resume pattern itself, which fits a daemon well — no external services are inherently required, the LangSmith/SaaS gating is a product choice, not an architectural one.

autogen.identity_model: Identity is agent-level, not human-user-level. In the v0.4 component model, every agent is a serializable component: provider string, component_type ('agent', 'tool', 'workbench', 'model', 'termination', ...), component_version, and a schema-validated config dict (ComponentModel in autogen_core._component_config). At the AgentChat layer, the ChatAgent protocol requires a 'name' that must be unique within a team plus a 'description' used by teams for routing decisions; messages carry a 'source' field (e.g. 'user', agent name). At the autogen-core layer, agents are addressed by AgentId(agent_type, agent_key). There is no built-in concept of an end-user principal, session owner, or per-user scoping — human users enter only as messages with source='user' or via UserProxyAgent. Docs also warn component deserialization must only load from trusted sources.
autogen.tool_scoping_mechanism: Scoping is purely constructor-injection: AssistantAgent(name, model_client, tools=[...]) executes the given tools itself (no separate executor since v0.4; tools are executed by the same agent inside run()). Tools are Python functions or BaseTool subclasses (ComponentBase with component_type='tool'); a Workbench (e.g. StaticWorkbench(tools=[...])) bundles tools that share state/resources and can expose a dynamic list_tools() that changes after each execution, and AssistantAgent can take a workbench. AgentTool wraps any BaseChatAgent as a tool. There is no declarative permission/ACL object attached to tools — an agent can call exactly what it was given.
autogen.permission_gating: No built-in permission system, no RBAC, no tool-approval gate — permission control is developer-supplied (choose the tools list, write wrapper tools that check authorization). Human-in-the-loop exists only as conversation control: (1) UserProxyAgent with an input_func blocks the team run until the user responds — docs explicitly warn this blocking 'holds up the team's progress and puts the team in an unstable state that cannot be saved or resumed', so it is recommended only for short immediate approvals; (2) handoff to a 'user' agent plus HandoffTermination stops the run when an agent hands off, letting the app persist team state and resume on the next run() with the human's feedback; (3) max_turns forces periodic stops. Approval is therefore turn-granular, not per-tool-call-gated by policy.
autogen.maturity: v0.4+ is documented as stable with full reference docs and a component serialization/versioning scheme, but the permission story is explicitly thin: component loading is trust-the-source, HITL mid-run is documented as unstable/blocking, and authorization is left to application code.
autogen.fit_assessment: Portable ideas for a single-daemon Go platform: (1) per-agent tool lists injected at agent construction is trivially portable to a Go registry and matches the simplest correct model — capability = what you hand the agent; (2) the Workbench abstraction (dynamic tool list that changes after executions, start/stop/reset lifecycle, save/load state) is a nice seam for runtime-gated tools; (3) the component model (provider + type + version + validated config) is a reasonable shape for serializable agent definitions. What NOT to copy: blocking in-run human input and the absence of any permission layer — a Go daemon should keep approvals out of the critical loop (persist and resume) and needs its own permission engine, which AutoGen offers no reference design for. AutoGen contributes less to identity/permission design than LangGraph; its main lesson is the negative one that large frameworks leave authorization to the application.

spiffe_spire.what_it_is: SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone) is a CNCF-graduated open standard that gives software workloads a cryptographically verifiable identity: a SPIFFE ID (spiffe://trust-domain/path) delivered in verifiable documents called SVIDs. SPIRE (SPIFFE Runtime Environment) is the reference implementation: a two-component system (SPIRE Server = signing authority/registry; SPIRE Agent = per-node daemon exposing the SPIFFE Workload API over a local Unix socket) that attests running software and issues/rotates SPIFFE IDs and SVIDs so workloads can do mTLS or sign/verify JWTs. Both SPIFFE and SPIRE are CNCF graduated projects. Spiffe.io is the documentation home; SPIRE currently has ~2.4k GitHub stars and production adopters including Uber, Netflix, Square, Pinterest, GitHub.
spiffe_spire.svid_and_attestation_summary: An SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document) is a short-lived credential that carries the SPIFFE ID. Three profiles exist in the Workload API spec: X.509-SVID (certificate with the SPIFFE ID as a URI SAN), JWT-SVID (short-lived signed JWT), and the optional WIT-SVID (Workload Identity Token). Workloads fetch SVIDs and the trust bundle from the SPIFFE Workload API (gRPC over a local socket) with no explicit secret — SPIRE determines the caller's identity via attestation. SPIRE attestation is two-phase: (1) node attestation — the agent proves the node's identity to the server via a trusted third party (AWS IID, Azure IMDS/MSI, GCP IIT, k8s PSAT, join_token, sshpop, tpm_devid, x509pop); (2) workload attestation — when a process calls the Workload API, the agent interrogates the local kernel/platform (UID/GID/path, Kubernetes namespace+service account, Docker labels, systemd unit, Slurm) via WorkloadAttestor plugins, converts the findings into selectors, and matches them against registration entries (spiffe ID + selectors + parentID) created on the server. Identity is 'earned, not assumed': a stolen static key cannot be replayed from elsewhere because identity binds to attested runtime properties. SVIDs rotate automatically (defaults commonly cited as ~1h for X.509-SVIDs, ~5min for JWT-SVIDs).

agent_identity_work_2025_2026.sig_status: CORRECTION TO THE TASK'S PREMISE: as of October 2026 there is NO 'SPIFFE Agentic AI SIG'. The spiffe/spiffe repository lists exactly three SIGs — SIG-Community, SIG-Spec, SIG-SPIRE (github.com/spiffe/spiffe README + community/ dir contains only sig-community, sig-spec, sig-spire). The 'sig-agentic-ai' that surfaces in searches is the CNOE (Cloud Native Operational Excellence) Agentic AI SIG (github.com/cnoe-io), a separate CNCF-affiliated vendor forum building the CAIPE multi-agent reference platform — not a SPIFFE project body. SPIFFE's agentic-AI work is happening inside SIG-Spec and via IETF WIMSE collaboration, not a dedicated SPIFFE SIG.
deliverables_2025_2026: SPIFFE Standard Roadmap blog (spiffe.io/blog/2026-08-18-spiffe-standard-roadmap/, Arndt Schwenkschuster, Aug 18 2026): explicitly names AI agents as a driver for three SIG-Spec work items — (a) Transaction Tokens (short-lived signed JWTs carrying who originated a request and on whose behalf an agent acts, targeting end-to-end security of agent call chains; experimental Workload API profile PR forthcoming), (b) a remote Workload API for environments that cannot host a SPIRE agent, explicitly including 'Managed AI-Agent platforms' (plus Lambda/Cloud Run/GitHub Actions), and (c) SPIFFE in open environments (.well-known-style trust-domain discovery for agents acting across trust boundaries). Also: SPIFFE Filesystem Delivery (spiffe/spiffe PR #376) and post-quantum JWT/WIT alg allowlist work.

SPIFFE Community Day 2026 (spiffe.io/community-day-2026/, 27 Oct 2026, London): 'SPIFFE and AIMS — A foundation for Agentic Identity' (Pieter Kasselman, Defakto) — the IETF WIMSE WG adopted the Agent Identity Management System (AIMS) model which points to SPIFFE as a critical layer of agentic identity; plus 'After the SVID: Emerging Authorization Patterns for SPIFFE Workloads and Agents' (Kevin Sapp, Aembit) covering SVIDs-as-OAuth-credentials, token exchange, Transaction Tokens, WIMSE, AuthZEN, AAuth.

IETF WIMSE agent auth: draft-klrc-aiagent-auth ('AI Agent Authentication and Authorization', a.k.a. AIMS; authors from Defakto, AWS, Zscaler, Ping, OpenAI, Okta) was adopted by the WIMSE WG (adoption call late Aug 2026; presented at WIMSE interim June 2026 and IETF 126). It requires each agent to have exactly one WIMSE identifier which MAY be a SPIFFE ID, requires short-lived primary credentials which may be SPIFFE SVIDs (X.509-SVID/JWT-SVID/WIT-SVID), and names SPIFFE as the mechanism for automated short-lived runtime provisioning. Related drafts: draft-ietf-wimse-identifier, draft-ietf-wimse-workload-creds, draft-ietf-wimse-wpt, draft-ietf-wimse-http-signature.

SPIRE issue #7077 (github.com/spiffe/spire/issues/7077, opened Jun 2026, open/blocked): proposes extending SPIRE JWT-SVID issuance with RFC 8693 OAuth token-exchange 'act' claims so a credential can carry sub=user + act.sub=agent for user-delegated agentic identity. States plainly: 'Today, neither SPIFFE nor SPIRE has primitives for expressing this [delegation] in an SVID.' Documents a path-encoded-SPIFFE-ID workaround vs. a spec amendment for act semantics.

Google Cloud 'Agent Identity' (docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/agent-identity-overview): production-scale SPIFFE-for-AI-agents shipped by Google — each agent gets a strongly attested SPIFFE ID (spiffe://TRUST_DOMAIN/resources/...) with auto-provisioned X.509 certs, mTLS to Google APIs, DPoP double-binding at the Agent Gateway, plus an auth manager for OAuth/API-key delegation; access tokens are cryptographically bound to the agent's X.509 certificate.

Google A2A protocol auth story (context): A2A deliberately delegates identity to standard web mechanisms — TLS, OAuth2/OIDC via AgentCard securitySchemes, credentials acquired out-of-band and sent in HTTP headers; payloads carry no identity (github.com/google/A2A docs/specification.md section 7; a2a-protocol.org/latest/topics/enterprise-ready/). No A2A+SPIFFE integration exists in the A2A spec itself; SPIFFE-A2A pairing appears only in third-party/community work (e.g. Microsoft's SPIFFE-based agent-identity research repo microsoft.github.io/identity-spiffe pairing a SPIFFE mTLS path with a direct A2A HTTPS path, and HashiCorp/Consul agentic demos).

Ecosystem commentary 2025: Solo.io/Christian Posta blog 'Agent Identity and Access Management — Can SPIFFE Work?' (Jun 26 2025) — yes in principle, but current K8s implementations give all replicas of an agent the same identity, a mismatch with agents' non-deterministic per-instance behavior; calls for instance-level agent identities. Riptides blog 'SPIFFE Meets OAuth2' (2025) — SVIDs presented directly as OAuth client authentication. AgenticTrust blog (Jun 30 2025) — extension patterns: instance-level IDs, delegation-chain tracking, context-aware identity. OpenID Foundation report 'Identity Management for Agentic AI' (arxiv.org/html/2510.25819, Tobin South, from Apr 2025) — SPIFFE/SPIRE is robust within controlled infrastructure but fundamentally relies on control of the host infrastructure for attestation, which limits portability across heterogeneous trust boundaries; agent identity also needs model/version/capability metadata and OAuth 2.1 delegation integration. Red Hat topic page and an ICCA 2025 paper ('SPIFFE-Based Zero-Trust Authentication for AI Agent Ecosystems') demonstrate SPIFFE mTLS replacing API keys for multi-agent frameworks on Kubernetes.

single_daemon_fit.verdict: Poor fit as an architecture; the identity FORMAT (SPIFFE ID + short-lived self-managed mTLS certs) is adoptable without SPIRE. Running SPIRE for one Go binary is disproportionate.
reasoning: SPIRE is a separate distributed service: a SPIRE Server (CA + registration registry + SQL datastore) plus a SPIRE Agent that must be installed and run on every node hosting an identified workload (spiffe.io/docs/latest/spire-about/spire-concepts/, use-cases page: install server, install agent per machine, configure node+workload attestation, create registration entries). For a single Go daemon (the consuming project's shape: one meept-daemon binary, no heavyweight external services) this adds two always-on processes, a datastore, a plugin/registration maintenance surface, and a bootstrap/attestation operational burden to protect exactly one identity — a security substrate that costs more than the asset it protects.

SPIRE's value proposition is attestation of processes you don't control on shared infrastructure — 'who is this process?' answered by interrogating the kernel/kubelet. A single self-owned daemon already knows what it is; the OS user, file permissions (0600 key material), and the existing dev_key/loopback-pairing model provide the same 'identity bound to the host' property with far less machinery. Workload attestation of your own binary by your own agent adds little assurance on a single-tenant host.

Architectural mismatch is acknowledged upstream: the Aug 2026 SPIFFE roadmap concedes 'SPIFFE only works when you control the host running the workload' and lists managed AI-agent platforms as a gap a future remote Workload API would address; the delegated-identity API exists precisely because some runtimes can't be attested directly. wasmCloud hit the same wall (SPIFFE expects to observe every workload; embedded runtimes need workarounds). A standalone daemon is the trivial degenerate case of this problem.

What IS worth borrowing is the pattern, not the service: a SPIFFE-ID-shaped identity for the daemon, short-lived automatically-rotated X.509 certs for mTLS with peers, and (if user-delegation ever matters) RFC 8693 act-claim semantics — noting SPIRE itself doesn't yet support act claims in JWT-SVIDs (issue #7077). A Go binary can self-issue or use any small CA for this; go-spiffe (github.com/spiffe/go-spiffe) can consume/verify SVIDs later if the deployment ever grows into SPIRE-managed infrastructure, making 'speak SPIFFE' a cheap forward-compatible wire format choice independent of running SPIRE.

Agent-specific gaps further weaken the case: SPIFFE/SPIRE has no delegation primitives yet (no act claims, no on-behalf-of user identity — SPIRE #7077; agentic-ai.readthedocs.io: 'the standard predates agents'), and community analyses (Solo.io, OpenID Foundation) agree SPIFFE today answers 'what workload is this' but not the agent-specific questions (which user, which instance, what capabilities).

alternatives: In-process short-lived self-managed mTLS: the daemon generates/holds a key, obtains short-lived certs from a lightweight CA (own CA, step-ca, or HashiCorp Vault PKI), auto-rotates — the SPIFFE SVID pattern minus server/agent/datastore. SPIFFE Filesystem Delivery (spiffe/spiffe PR #376) is standardizing exactly this file-based credential interface, so a daemon following it stays interoperable.

go-spiffe library without a SPIRE deployment: use go-spiffe helpers to produce/verify SPIFFE-ID-formatted X.509/JWT credentials issued by any CA, keeping the wire format forward-compatible with future SPIRE adoption.

Cloud vendor workload identity where available: Google Agent Identity (SPIFFE-based, managed, purpose-built for AI agents), AWS SPIFFE-compatible roles-anywhere / IRSA-style token exchange — replaces self-hosting SPIRE with a managed issuer, though it ties the daemon to that cloud.

OAuth 2.0 mTLS-bound credentials / RFC 8705 (certificate-bound tokens) or DPoP (RFC 9449): proof-of-possession tokens bound to a key the daemon holds — the approach Google Agent Identity uses beyond its mTLS gateway and the direction MCP/A2A ecosystems are converging on (OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents, token exchange RFC 8693 with act claims for user-delegation).

IETF WIMSE-aligned primitives as they land: WIMSE Workload Identity Tokens (WIT) and Workload Proof Tokens (WPT), Transaction Tokens (draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens) for on-behalf-of context — implementable in-process as JWT signing with a local key, no external service required.

Static-key-plus-TLS status quo (what meept does today with dev_key + loopback pairing): adequate for a single-daemon, single-trust-boundary deployment; upgrade path is the self-managed short-lived-cert pattern above rather than SPIRE.

citations.claim: SPIRE is a two-component system (server = signing authority + registry; agent per node) that performs node and workload attestation to issue SVIDs
SVIDs come in X.509-SVID, JWT-SVID and optional WIT-SVID profiles and are delivered via the SPIFFE Workload API with no explicit secret; SPIRE authenticates the caller by inspecting kernel metadata

Workload attestation interrogates the node kernel/platform for the calling process's properties and matches them against registration-entry selectors; node attestation uses cloud/k8s/TPM/x509/join-token trusted third parties
Built-in attestor plugins: aws_iid, azure_imds/msi, gcp_iit, k8s_psat, join_token, sshpop, tpm_devid, x509pop (node); unix, k8s, docker, systemd, slurm (workload)
Deploying SPIRE for mTLS requires installing a server, an agent on each machine, configuring attestation, creating registration entries, and wiring workloads to the Workload API
The Workload API has three profiles (X.509-SVID and JWT-SVID mandatory, WIT-SVID optional)
SPIFFE and SPIRE are CNCF graduated projects; SPIRE 'exposes the SPIFFE Workload API, which can attest running software systems and issue SPIFFE IDs and SVIDs'
As of Oct 2026 spiffe/spiffe lists only three SIGs (SIG-Community, SIG-Spec, SIG-SPIRE) — no Agentic AI SIG; SIG material lives in /community (sig-community, sig-spec, sig-spire only)
The sig-agentic-ai found in search is the CNOE forum's Agentic AI SIG (CAIPE multi-agent platform), not a SPIFFE body

SPIFFE SIG-Spec's 2026-2027 roadmap names AI agents as motivation for Transaction Tokens, a remote Workload API explicitly covering 'Managed AI-Agent platforms', and .well-known-style open-environment trust-domain discovery
The roadmap states 'SPIFFE only works when you control the host running the workload', excluding lambda/managed-agent-platform deployment patterns
SPIFFE Community Day 2026 (27 Oct 2026) features 'SPIFFE and AIMS — a foundation for Agentic Identity' and a talk on post-SVID authorization patterns for agents

IETF WIMSE adopted draft-klrc-aiagent-auth (AIMS): each agent MUST have exactly one WIMSE identifier which MAY be a SPIFFE ID; credentials may be SPIFFE SVIDs; SPIFFE is the named provisioning mechanism
draft-klrc-aiagent-auth maps existing standards (WIMSE, OAuth 2.0, SPIFFE) to agent authentication rather than defining a new protocol
SPIRE issue #7077: neither SPIFFE nor SPIRE has primitives for expressing user-delegation (RFC 8693 act claims) in an SVID; proposes JWT-SVID act-claim support for agentic identity
Google Cloud Agent Identity gives each AI agent a strongly attested SPIFFE ID with auto-provisioned X.509 certs, mTLS + DPoP double binding, and an auth manager for delegated OAuth

wasmCloud needed SPIRE's delegated-identity API because SPIFFE 'expects to be able to observe every workload it issues identities for' — attestation assumes direct process visibility
Agentic-AI reference material summarizes the gaps: SPIFFE standard predates agents, defines no user-delegation representation, and attestation strength depends entirely on the chosen SPIRE plugins

consensus: None of the surveyed frameworks (OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph/LangChain, AutoGen, Semantic Kernel) ships a built-in identity or permission engine; all four delegate authorization to the host application. LangGraph is the furthest along (platform-level @auth middleware + resource-level filters), and even that is Python/SaaS-gated.

The universal scoping primitive is constructor-injection of a tool list per agent (OpenAI Agent(tools=[...]), LangGraph bind_tools/create_agent(tools=[...]), AutoGen AssistantAgent(tools=[...]), SK plugin imports per Kernel, MCP per-server connection). Group-based ACLs on top of a shared tool registry would be a step beyond what any mainstream framework offers.

Per-tool authorization in MCP does NOT exist at the protocol level (server-level OAuth 2.1 resource-server model only); every vendor (WorkOS, Scalekit, Auth0) implements per-tool gating as application-layer checks. A Go platform should do the same rather than wait for the spec.

Human-in-the-loop approval patterns converge on pause/persist/resume (LangGraph interrupt+checkpointer, OpenAI paused runs, AutoGen HandoffTermination) rather than blocking mid-run —meept's plans approve/reject + ACP relay already match this.

For agent identity, the standards direction is SPIFFE-ID-shaped identifiers + short-lived credentials + delegation semantics (IETF WIMSE AIMS draft, Transaction Tokens, RFC 8693 act claims) — all implementable in-process without running SPIRE.
recommended_posture_for_meept: Adopt github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk (v1.8.0) for MCP client/server transport+session plumbing; stdio servers need no OAuth.

Implement authorization in-process: per-group tool allowlists over the internal/tools registry (the constructor-injection pattern every framework uses), per-tool required-permission checks in tool handlers (the universal vendor pattern), and optional server-level bearer-token checking via the SDK's RequireBearerToken when exposing MCP endpoints.

Borrow LangGraph's owner-stamping + read-filter and namespace-prefix-forcing patterns for memory scopes; borrow SK's ordered filter pipeline (explicit ordered slice, not map) as the tool-dispatch middleware shape; return meaningful refusal messages to the model on denied calls (SK consent-filter pattern) so agents don't blind-retry.

Do not run SPIRE. If agent-to-agent mTLS is ever needed, use the SPIFFE ID format with self-managed short-lived certs (go-spiffe compatible), which stays forward-compatible with SPIRE-managed deployments and the WIMSE AIMS direction.
